paras: Thread cleaning and inspection is one of the most understated steps in a casing program, and one of the most consequential. When this work is done right, casing runs are predictable. When it is skipped or rushed, problems show up after the cement has set.

intro: Every casing job runs through the same standard sequence:

steps.title: Receiving and Layout
steps.text: Pipe is received, laid out, and prepared for inspection. Every joint is accounted for before the work starts.

steps.title: Visual and Gauge Inspection
steps.text: Each connection is inspected for damage, corrosion, and handling marks. Gauge inspection confirms the connection is within manufacturer spec.

steps.title: Cleaning
steps.text: Pin and box ends are cleaned to remove debris, mill scale, and old thread compound. Connections are prepared for proper make-up.

steps.title: Laser Tally and Documentation
steps.text: Every joint is logged, measured, and confirmed. The operator receives a complete tally and inspection report before the run begins.

sections.title: Why this matters
paras: Every casing connection is a pressure seal. It has to transfer load, resist fatigue, and hold up to the conditions of the wellbore for the life of the well. That performance depends on clean, undamaged threads that mate the way the manufacturer designed them to.

Debris, corrosion, storage damage, or leftover thread compound can compromise make-up. On the rig floor, under time pressure, these problems are easy to miss. The result is wasted connections, rework, or worse: integrity issues that surface after the casing is cemented.
Thread cleaning and inspection removes that variable. It gives the crew a known starting point and gives the operator documented evidence that the program started with sound pipe.
sections.quote: “The small step that protects the rest of the program. Done in daylight before the run, not after the cement has set.”
